title: From Outcomes to Steps: Reliable Success-Aware Critic Learning for Long-Horizon Language Agents

paper.title: From Outcomes to Steps: Reliable Success-Aware Critic Learning for Long-Horizon Language Agents
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reinforcement learning for long-horizon language agents requires identifying whether intermediate actions make eventual task success more or less likely when supervision is available only at trajectory level.
The main difficulty is that a critic with aggregate return-prediction accuracy may still fail to resolve the local value differences needed to assign credit to actions , especially under sparse feedback and function approximation. Conventional critics estimate future return, but policy improvement also depends on knowing whether each intermediate decision makes task success more or less likely.
We introduce SCALE , an actor–critic framework that augments conventional return estimation with explicit prediction of eventual task success. At each interaction prefix, the critic predicts a return value and a Success Value , defined as the probability that the task will eventually be completed from that prefix. SCALE converts changes in Success Value into multi-step action credit through Success-GAE and modulates its contribution according to the estimated reliability of the predictor, while retaining the token-level PPO objective.
Across five agent benchmarks and three model backbones, SCALE improves task performance over the compared RL baselines in most settings, with gains of up to 4.1 percentage points in success rate. Separate critic-learning analyses show that SCALE also improves critic estimation and training stability.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Comparison between PPO and SCALE . PPO derives step credit from changes in predicted return, which can be unreliable when feedback is sparse. An action may receive positive credit even when it lowers the probability of eventual success. SCALE instead uses changes in Success Value to measure whether each action makes task success more or less likely. Large language models (LLMs) are deployed as interactive agents that browse the web, use tools, and interact with environments over many steps ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Shridhar et al., 2021 ; Yao et al., 2022 ) . Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a framework for improving such agents from task outcomes ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Feng et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026b ) , yet it remains difficult to tell which intermediate actions help or hurt the outcome. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , an action can satisfy a local constraint yet make the task less likely to succeed. The learner therefore needs to determine which intermediate decisions improve the prospect of eventual task completion. For long-horizon language agents, this is difficult because supervision often arrives only after the entire interaction, while policy improvement depends on distinguishing the effects of individual decisions along the way. Existing methods assign credit at different parts of the trajectory. Standard PPO and outcome-based methods optimize token probabilities from trajectory-level returns ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) , while recent methods assign credit to individual turns or environment actions ( Zeng et al., 2025 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Ding et al., 2026 ) . Critic-based methods further estimate intermediate values to propagate delayed outcomes ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Kazemnejad et al., 2025 ; Hou et al., 2026 ) . These methods assign credit at finer parts of the trajectory, but accurate prediction of future return does not necessarily imply reliable action-level credit. Under sparse supervision and function approximation, a change in predicted return may not tell us whether a particular action made eventual success more likely. The central issue is therefore not only where credit is assigned, but whether the critic preserves the local ordering between alternative actions and whether its reliability can be assessed during training . In Sec. 3.2 , we show that this concern is practical rather than hypothetical, conventional PPO critics produce action-level credit that degrades toward random chance at long horizons and remains unstable throughout training, leaving reliable critic learning for long-horizon credit assignment an open challenge. To address these challenges, we introduce SCALE ( S uccess- C alibrated A dvantage L earning and E stimation), a success-aware actor–critic framework for long-horizon language agents. SCALE makes eventual task completion an explicit prediction target alongside conventional return estimation, rather than relying on return alone . Specifically, the critic retains a return head for expected cumulative reward and adds a Success Value head that estimates the probability of satisfying the benchmark’s terminal completion criterion from the current interaction prefix. It then uses changes in this prediction to assign credit to individual environment steps, reflecting whether each action improves eventual success. Because the reliability of this signal can vary during training, SCALE adjusts its contribution according to critic quality. The resulting credit complements the standard return-based advantage while retaining the token-level PPO objective. Sec. 4 details the framework. We evaluate SCALE on five representative agentic benchmarks spanning text-based interaction and tool use: ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ) , WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) , ScienceWorld ( Wang et al., 2022 ) , BFCL-v4 ( Patil et al., 2025 ) , and AppWorld ( Trivedi et al., 2024 ) . Across these tasks, SCALE consistently outperforms most strong agentic RL baselines and delivers substantial gains in task performance. Beyond end-task performance, We also analyze critic quality and the accuracy of its action credit to understand where these gains come from. Our contributions are threefold: ❶ Local-credit failure of return critics. We show that conventional PPO critics become less reliable at distinguishing alternative actions as decisions move farther from terminal supervision. ❷ Success-Based Credit with Reliability Control. We introduce SCALE , which explicitly predicts eventual task success from each interaction prefix and converts changes in this probability into multi-step action credit . It then modulates the contribution of this credit according to estimated critic reliability , while retaining the standard token-level PPO objective. ❸ Empirical validation. Experiments across five agent benchmarks and three model backbones show improvements in task performance, including gains of up to 4.1 percentage points in success rate. Additional analyses show improved action ranking and support the roles of success-based credit and reliability control.

sections.heading: Reinforcement Learning for LLM-based Agents.
sections.text: Reinforcement learning has evolved from preference alignment ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ) toward optimization from verifiable task outcomes ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , and has recently been extended to interactive language agents. Existing work studies RL for search and tool use ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Feng et al., 2026 ; Qian et al., 2025 ) , multi-turn environment interaction ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026b ) , and general agent-training frameworks ( Feng et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) . Scalable RL infrastructures such as verl ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) and ROLL ( Wang et al., 2025a ) support large-scale rollout generation and environment interaction. Other approaches improve long-horizon learning through planning and exploration ( Paglieri et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026d ; Wang et al., 2026c ) . While these methods improve the training and exploration of language agents, a central challenge remains: how to convert sparse trajectory-level outcomes into reliable credit for intermediate actions , particularly for decisions far from terminal supervision.

sections.heading: Credit Assignment and Critic Learning.
sections.text: Existing approaches differ along two dimensions that are central to credit assignment: where credit is assigned along a trajectory and how that credit is estimated. Critic-free methods derive turn- or step-level signals through comparison, grouping, or structural information ( Zeng et al., 2025 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026d ) , but often require repeated states, milestones, or other task-dependent structure. Monte Carlo methods estimate local action values from multiple continuations, avoiding a learned critic at the cost of substantial sampling overhead ( Kazemnejad et al., 2025 ) . Critic-based methods instead propagate delayed outcomes through learned turn- or action-level values ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Tan et al., 2026 ) , but reliable local comparisons remain difficult when value estimates are learned from sparse supervision. Recent work further improves robustness by suppressing unreliable updates or controlling the use of uncertain credit signals ( Li et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2026b ; Tao et al., 2026 ) . In contrast, SCALE explicitly predicts eventual task success from each interaction prefix and uses the estimated reliability of this prediction to control its contribution to environment-step credit. sections.heading: 3.2 Analysis
sections.text: We first ask whether a PPO critic can provide reliable local credit for long-horizon agent decisions. For policy improvement, the critic must do more than predict return: it must rank alternative actions correctly. This ranking is hard to learn from a limited number of rollouts when feedback is sparse, especially for decisions far from the terminal outcome ( Li et al., 2025b ; Kazemnejad et al., 2025 ) . To test this directly, we start from the same interaction prefix, sample different candidate actions, and roll out each action several times. For each prefix h t h_{t} , we estimate a Monte Carlo state value V ^ MC ​ ( h t ) = M − 1 ​ ∑ m G t ( m ) \hat{V}_{\mathrm{MC}}(h_{t})=M^{-1}\sum_{m}G_{t}^{(m)} . We further sample K K candidate actions and evaluate each with M M continuations, yielding Q ^ MC R ​ ( h t , a t ( j ) ) = M − 1 ​ ∑ m G t ( j , m ) \hat{Q}_{\mathrm{MC}}^{R}(h_{t},a_{t}^{(j)})=M^{-1}\sum_{m}G_{t}^{(j,m)} . We measure critic estimation with explained variance and local credit quality with pairwise ordering accuracy between the critic score Q ^ V ​ ( h t , a t ) = r t + γ ⁡ ( 1 − d t ) ​ V ψ ​ ( h t + 1 ) \hat{Q}_{V}(h_{t},a_{t})=r_{t}+\gamma(1-d_{t})V_{\psi}(h_{t+1}) and the Monte Carlo action values. Prefixes are divided into Near , Mid , and Far according to benchmark-specific tertiles of the remaining horizon H t = T − t H_{t}=T-t . Figure 2: Vanilla PPO critic reliability analysis on ALFWorld and WebShop. Observation 1: Critic estimation degrades with horizon. Figure 2 (a) shows a consistent drop in explained variance from near to far horizon prefixes across both benchmarks, indicating that return estimation becomes less reliable as decisions move farther from outcome supervision. Observation 2: Local action credit degrades more critically. Figure 2 (b) shows that pairwise action ordering accuracy decreases with horizon and approaches the random baseline for far horizon. This result shows that the critic’s ordering increasingly diverges from Monte Carlo estimates for decisions farther from terminal outcome. Thus, even a critic with nontrivial return-prediction ability may fail to distinguish better actions, consistent with prior findings on learned value models ( Kazemnejad et al., 2025 ) . Observation 3: Credit quality changes throughout training. Figure 2 (c) shows that action-ordering accuracy improves overall, but it does not improve steadily across updates. Fig. 2 (d) shows that critic value loss initially decreases but later rebounds and fluctuates, showing that critic quality remains unstable throughout training rather than improving steadily with policy updates. Together, these results show a limitation of the standard return critic: its action rankings become less reliable for decisions far from the final outcome and can fluctuate during training. This motivates adding a direct success signal and using it only when the critic is reliable.

sections.heading: 4.1 Overview
sections.text: As illustrated in Fig. 3 , SCALE addresses the gap between return prediction and reliable credit assignment in long trajectories. While return critics can implicitly encode task success, this signal may be unreliable for local credit assignment in practice. SCALE therefore augments the return critic with an Success Value head. Success-GAE uses changes in this prediction to compute step credit, and SCALE scales this credit according to the reliability of the success critic. The resulting step advantage is finally broadcast to all tokens of the corresponding action for token-level PPO optimization. Figure 3: Overview of SCALE . Top: A simple rollout example contrasts an ideal return critic with practical training, where sparse supervision and imperfect learning make reliable action-level credit difficult. Bottom: SCALE learns success-aware critic signals, converts them into reliable environment-step credit, and uses the resulting advantages for token-level policy optimization.

sections.heading: 4.2 Success-Aware Dual-Head Critic
sections.text: The preceding analysis suggests that accurate return estimation alone may not provide reliable local credit for eventual task success. We therefore augment the conventional return critic with an explicit success-prediction head. Given an interaction prefix h t h_{t} , the dual-head critic outputs 𝒞 ⁡ ( h t ) = ( V ψ ​ ( h t ) , P ϕ ​ ( h t ) ) \mathcal{C}(h_{t})=\big(V_{\psi}(h_{t}),P_{\phi}(h_{t})\big) , where V ψ ​ ( h t ) V_{\psi}(h_{t}) estimates future return and P ϕ ​ ( h t ) P_{\phi}(h_{t}) denotes the Success Value defined in Sec. 3.1 . The return head predicts expected future reward. The success head predicts whether the task will eventually be completed from the current prefix. To jointly learn these two signals from collected trajectories, we optimize return regression together with success prediction: ℒ critic = 𝔼 τ ​ [ 1 T ​ ∑ t = 0 T − 1 ( ( V ψ ​ ( h t ) − G ^ t ) 2 + η S ​ BCE ​ ( P ϕ ​ ( h t ) , S ) ) ] . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{critic}}=\mathbb{E}_{\tau}\left[\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\left(\big(V_{\psi}(h_{t})-\hat{G}_{t}\big)^{2}+\eta_{S}\,\mathrm{BCE}\!\left(P_{\phi}(h_{t}),S\right)\right)\right]. (2) Here, G ^ t \hat{G}_{t} is the return target for prefix h t h_{t} , S S is the trajectory-level success label, and η S \eta_{S} balances return regression and success prediction. Because each interaction prefix is paired with the eventual task outcome, the success head directly learns to predict eventual task completion from that prefix, rather than relying on this information to emerge implicitly from return fitting. This explicit Success Value will serve as the basis for constructing success-aware environment-step credit in the next stage.

sections.heading: 4.3 Success-GAE
sections.text: The Success Value is defined on interaction prefixes, but policy learning requires credit for the action that moves the agent from h t h_{t} to h t + 1 h_{t+1} . We therefore turn successive success predictions into an action-level signal. Let p t = P ϕ ​ ( h t ) p_{t}=P_{\phi}(h_{t}) and set the terminal prediction to the observed outcome, p T = S p_{T}=S . We define the success temporal difference as δ t S = p t + 1 − p t \delta_{t}^{S}=p_{t+1}-p_{t} : an action receives positive credit when it increases the predicted probability of eventual success and negative credit when it decreases it. A single temporal difference captures only the immediate change in success prospects, whereas long-horizon actions may influence several subsequent steps. We therefore aggregate future success differences in the same spirit as generalized advantage estimation and define Success-GAE as A ^ t S = ∑ l = 0 T − t − 1 λ S l ​ δ t + l S , λ S ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] . \hat{A}_{t}^{S}=\sum_{l=0}^{T-t-1}\lambda_{S}^{l}\delta_{t+l}^{S},\qquad\lambda_{S}\in[0,1]. (3) Here, A ^ t S \hat{A}_{t}^{S} is the success-oriented advantage for action a t a_{t} , δ t + l S \delta_{t+l}^{S} measures subsequent changes in predicted success, and λ S \lambda_{S} controls how strongly later changes contribute to the current action. Unlike return-based GAE, Success-GAE does not use the environment discount factor because it tracks changes in task-success probability rather than accumulated reward. The resulting signal assigns credit based on whether intermediate decisions make eventual success more or less likely.

sections.heading: 4.5 Token-Level Policy Optimization
sections.text: To optimize the autoregressive policy, we assign this advantage to all tokens in the action and retain the standard token-level clipped PPO objective ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) . Thus, SCALE augments the action advantage with reliability-weighted success credit while leaving the PPO actor objective unchanged. Appendix A provides a theoretical analysis of when the added success signal can improve the distinction between actions.

sections.heading: Benchmarks.
sections.text: We evaluate SCALE on five long-horizon agentic benchmarks spanning two major interaction paradigms. ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ) , WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) , and ScienceWorld ( Wang et al., 2022 ) represent text-based interactive environments, covering embodied household tasks, web navigation, and scientific reasoning. BFCL-v4 ( Patil et al., 2025 ) and AppWorld ( Trivedi et al., 2024 ) evaluate tool-using agents through function calling and application-level execution. These benchmarks let us test SCALE across different interaction structures, action spaces, and task horizons. Full benchmark details are provided in Appendix C .

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare SCALE against representative prompting and RL baselines. Closed-source references include GPT-4o ( OpenAI, 2024 ) and Gemini-2.5-Pro ( Comanici et al., 2025 ) . Prompting baselines include Direct Prompt, ReAct ( Yao et al., 2023 ) , and Reflexion ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) . RL baselines cover three categories: (1) Standard policy optimization, including PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) , RLOO ( Ahmadian et al., 2024 ) , GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , and GSPO ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) ; (2) Fine-grained or structured credit assignment, including GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) , BEACON ( Wang et al., 2026d ) , ST-PPO ( Li et al., 2025a ) , and CAPO ( Wang et al., 2026a ) ; and (3) Critic-free sequence-level optimization, represented by SeeUPO ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . We use official implementations or closely follow the reported configurations whenever available.

sections.heading: Implementation.
sections.text: Our experiments use Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , together with Qwen3-8B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , as backbone models. ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld are implemented with verl-agent ( Feng et al., 2025 ) , while BFCL-v4 and AppWorld are built on AgentEvolver ( Zhai et al., 2025 ) . We retain Qwen2.5 due to more stable agentic performance and infrastructure support, and use the same base model across RL methods for fair comparison. Within each backbone and benchmark setting, all trainable methods share the same initial model, rollout budget, environment interface, and evaluation protocol. Detailed configurations and hyperparameters are provided in Appendix C .

sections.heading: Text-Based Interactive Benchmarks.
sections.text: Table 2 reports results on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop. With Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, SCALE reaches success rates of 93.4% on ALFWorld, 46.8% on ScienceWorld, and 78.1% on WebShop, exceeding the strongest RL baselines by 2.0, 1.5, and 1.5 percentage points, respectively. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, SCALE further improves to 97.4%, 66.5%, and 83.8%, with gains of 2.9, 2.2, and 4.1 percentage points over the strongest baselines. These gains appear across all three text-interaction benchmarks and both model sizes, indicating that the benefit of SCALE is not limited to a single environment or backbone scale. sections.heading: Tool-Use Benchmarks.
sections.text: Table 3 evaluates SCALE on AppWorld and BFCL-v4 with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B. SCALE achieves the best average performance across the two benchmarks with both backbones, reaching avg@4/pass@4 scores of 43.57/56.01 with Qwen2.5-7B and 50.44/62.47 with Qwen3-8B. On BFCL-v4, SCALE obtains 44.25/55.00 and 51.75/57.00, respectively, outperforming all compared RL baselines. On AppWorld, SCALE achieves the highest avg@4 with Qwen2.5-7B and the highest pass@4 with Qwen3-8B, while remaining close to SeeUPO on the other metric. Overall, the gains extend from text-interaction benchmarks to tool-use environments.

sections.heading: Episode Length.
sections.text: Figure 5 compares the average episode length on the three text-interaction benchmarks. SCALE reduces the number of environment steps from 27.6 to 19.1 on ALFWorld and from 19.7 to 13.2 on ScienceWorld, while remaining close to GiGPO on WebShop (6.9 vs. 6.8). Together with the task results, this suggests that SCALE achieves better outcomes with fewer interaction steps, avoiding unnecessarily long action sequences rather than relying on extended exploration. sections.heading: Training Efficiency.
sections.text: Figure 5 compares wall-clock time per training iteration on BFCL-v4 and AppWorld. Although SCALE adds a success head and reliability estimation, its training cost remains close to GRPO and GiGPO and is much lower than SeeUPO. This provides the performance gains without a large increase in training cost, suggesting that the additional critic computation introduces only modest practical overhead. Its critic loss decreases more smoothly and remains lower, whereas PPO shows larger fluctuations or later increases in several settings. These results suggest that adding the success signal helps the critic learn more stable and informative value estimates, with the same pattern across interaction settings. sections.heading: Training Performance.
sections.text: The improved critic dynamics are accompanied by stronger policy learning. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, SCALE reaches higher training success rates than PPO, while on BFCL-v4 and AppWorld it achieves consistently higher avg@4 . The performance gap also tends to widen over training, suggesting that better critic learning translates into more effective long-horizon policy optimization rather than merely better value fitting.

sections.heading: Ablation Study.
sections.text: Table 4 shows that removing any of the tested components lowers the performance of SCALE . Removing the Success Value head lowers avg@4 from 51.75 to 43.25 on BFCL-v4 and from 49.12 to 39.91 on AppWorld, while removing the return head causes larger drops to 29.75 and 20.18. Replacing multi-step success credit with one-step TD also degrades performance to 39.75 and 31.14. Finally, using only Brier score or explained variance remains below the full method on both benchmarks, supporting their combined use for reliability-aware integration. Overall, the results show that return estimation, success-based credit, and reliability weighting each play a distinct role in the full framework.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced SCALE for credit assignment in long-horizon language agents. Our analysis shows that a critic can retain aggregate return-prediction quality while becoming less reliable at ranking actions, especially for decisions far from terminal supervision. SCALE addresses this gap by predicting eventual task success, converting changes in this probability into multi-step action credit, and controlling its contribution according to predictor reliability. Across five agent benchmarks and three model backbones, SCALE improves task performance, while maintaining modest training overhead. These results show that improving local credit quality can benefit long-horizon policy learning without changing the underlying token-level PPO objective. Future work could explore incorporating richer signals into critic learning to improve reliability under long-horizon supervision.

sections.heading: Summary.
sections.text: The analysis gives three results. First, Success-GAE estimates eventual success without changing its expectation when the Success Critic is exact, and its error remains bounded when the critic is approximate. Second, this error determines when the expected ordering of two actions is preserved. Third, if the success signal is more accurate and less variable than the return signal, adding it can improve the separation between actions and tighten the bound on local action selection.

sections.heading: Appendix B Details of the Benchmarks
sections.text: We evaluate SCALE on five benchmarks spanning household interaction, web navigation, scientific experimentation, function calling, and application-level tool use. ALFWorld. ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ) is a text-based environment derived from ALFRED ( Shridhar et al., 2020 ) and TextWorld ( Côté et al., 2018 ) . An agent receives natural-language observations and must complete household tasks by navigating rooms and manipulating objects through textual commands. The benchmark includes tasks such as picking up, cleaning, heating, cooling, and examining objects. We use the standard benchmark split and report task success rate. WebShop. WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) simulates online shopping over a large collection of real products. Given a natural-language instruction, an agent searches for products, navigates product pages, selects options, and attempts to purchase an item that satisfies the requested attributes. The environment provides a graded task score based on how well the selected product matches the instruction, together with a binary success signal. We report both task score and success rate. ScienceWorld. ScienceWorld ( Wang et al., 2022 ) contains interactive science tasks in which an agent performs experiments and manipulates objects through natural-language actions. The tasks cover topics from physics, chemistry, and biology and require several dependent steps before the goal can be completed. We evaluate across the benchmark tasks and report both task score and success rate. BFCL-v4. BFCL-v4 ( Patil et al., 2025 ) evaluates the ability of language models to use external functions correctly. The agent must interpret a user request, choose appropriate functions, provide valid arguments, and use function outputs when further actions are required. This setting tests whether a policy can make reliable tool-use decisions over multiple interaction steps. We follow the benchmark evaluation protocol and report avg@4 together with pass@4 . AppWorld. AppWorld ( Trivedi et al., 2024 ) evaluates agents on tasks which interacts with APIs exposed by simulated applications. An agent must determine which applications and APIs are needed, execute sequences of calls, and use the returned information to complete the request. The tasks require dependent operations across applications, making successful completion sensitive to earlier decisions. We follow the standard evaluation protocol and report avg@4 together with pass@4 .

sections.heading: Appendix C Details of the Frameworks
sections.text: Our experiments cover two forms of agent interaction and therefore use two established training frameworks. For ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, we build on verl-agent ( Feng et al., 2025 ) and follow the environment implementation provided by BEACON ( Wang et al., 2026d ) . For BFCL-v4 and AppWorld, we use the environment and rollout setup released with AgentEvolver ( Zhai et al., 2025 ) and its SeeUPO implementation ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . We keep the environment interface, interaction protocol, and evaluation procedure of the corresponding framework, while replacing the policy-optimization component when evaluating different RL methods.

sections.heading: Text-based interaction framework.
sections.text: ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld are implemented with the interaction pipeline inherited from verl-agent. The framework separates language generation from environment execution: at each environment step, the model receives the task context and the latest environment observation, generates one complete action, and then passes this action to the environment. The next observation is returned only after the action has been executed. This interface matches the environment-step formulation used by SCALE , while the policy itself remains autoregressive at the token level. We use the environment implementations from the BEACON codebase for all three benchmarks. BEACON extends verl-agent with support for ScienceWorld while retaining the same interaction structure for ALFWorld and WebShop. The environment manager also records information produced at each transition, such as observations, executed actions, rewards, and episode termination. We use these trajectories to construct the return and success targets required by the two critic heads. No additional intermediate annotation is introduced by SCALE .

sections.heading: Interaction context.
sections.text: For the three text-based environments, the model input is constructed at every environment step rather than by treating the entire episode as one generated sequence. The input contains the task description, the current observation, a limited record of previous observations and actions, and the actions that are valid in the current state when the environment provides them. This follows the prompt and memory interface of verl-agent. The resulting structure keeps the correspondence between one model response and one environment action explicit. The three environments use the same general interaction pattern, while adapting the prompt to the task and action space. sections.heading: Tool-use interaction framework.
sections.text: For BFCL-v4 and AppWorld, we follow the training setup in the SeeUPO branch of AgentEvolver ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . In this framework, the RL trainer and the benchmark environment communicate through an environment service. The trainer sends the current interaction state and the generated action to this service, which executes the requested function or code and returns the resulting observation. This separation allows the same policy-training pipeline to interact with both benchmarks without embedding their execution logic in the optimizer. Following the reference setting, BFCL-v4 and AppWorld use asynchronous vLLM rollouts with at most 10 interaction steps, eight rollouts per prompt, and temperature 0.9 0.9 . We retain the framework’s linear think context template and keep the rollout protocol fixed across backbones. For BFCL-v4 ( Patil et al., 2025 ) , we use the multi-turn data and environment implementation in AgentEvolver. At each turn, the model receives the user request and currently available function definitions, generates a function call, and uses the returned execution result in the next turn. The implementation follows the Qwen function-call format shown below. Prompt Template for BFCL-v4 # Tools You may call one or more functions to assist with the user query. Evaluation uses the BFCL evaluation routines provided by the framework. For AppWorld ( Trivedi et al., 2024 ) , we use the official environment and evaluator wrapped by AgentEvolver. sections.heading: Consistency across methods.
sections.text: Within each benchmark and backbone, all RL methods use the same environment implementation, prompt format, rollout interface, and evaluation procedure. The differences between methods are restricted to their learning objectives and the quantities required by those objectives. In particular, SCALE does not introduce additional environment feedback or privileged intermediate supervision. Its Success Critic is trained from the same terminal task outcome that is available in the collected trajectories.

sections.heading: Appendix D Training Procedure of SCALE
sections.text: This section summarizes the training procedure of SCALE . At each iteration, the current policy collects trajectories, the dual-head critic learns return and success prediction from the same rollout data, and the resulting return- and success-based advantages are combined according to Success Critic reliability before the standard token-level PPO update. Algorithm 1 gives the complete procedure. sections.heading: Appendix E Case Studies of SCALE
sections.text: To complement the quantitative results in the main paper, we present two successful trajectories from ScienceWorld and BFCL-v4. These examples show why credit assignment is difficult in long-horizon tasks. An action may have a simple immediate effect, while its importance becomes clear only after later interactions. In ScienceWorld, the agent must complete several task requirements in the correct order. In BFCL-v4, actions in early turns change the filesystem used in later turns. We report the environment observations, actions, scores, user requests, and tool outputs.

sections.heading: E.1 ScienceWorld: Ordered Subgoals and Delayed Task Completion
sections.text: We first show a successful find-living-thing trajectory from ScienceWorld ( Wang et al., 2022 ) . The task contains several ordered requirements. The agent must first focus on a living thing and then move it to the orange box in the kitchen. As a result, the value of an early action depends on what the agent does in later steps. The trajectory below reports the actions, observations, and native ScienceWorld scores. Environment (Initial State) Task: Find a living thing. First, focus on the thing. Then, move it to the orange box in the kitchen. Agent (Step 1) <think> I first need to identify a living thing in the current environment. This location is called the outside. You see a blue jay egg, a butterfly egg, a dove egg, an axe, and a door to the kitchen. Agent (Step 2) <think> I can now see several eggs, which are possible living things for this task. The blue jay egg is a clear candidate, so I will use it as the target. sections.heading: Credit-assignment perspective.
sections.text: The focus action is important because it satisfies a required part of the task before the agent moves the object. Its effect cannot be judged from that step alone. The agent must still pick up the blue jay, move to the kitchen, and place it in the orange box. This example shows why an intermediate action should be evaluated by how it affects the chance of completing the full task. In SCALE, the Success Value estimates this probability from each interaction prefix, and changes in the Success Value provide the signal used by Success-GAE.

sections.heading: Credit-assignment perspective.
sections.text: The mkdir and mv calls in the first turn prepare the filesystem for the later requests. After final_report.pdf is moved to temp , later turns access the same file with grep and sort . The file is also used in the final diff operation. The importance of the first-turn actions therefore becomes clear only after several later turns. This example shows that credit for an early tool call may depend on whether the state it creates supports successful completion of later requests.

sections.heading: Discussion.
sections.text: The two examples show two common sources of delayed credit. In ScienceWorld, an early action satisfies one requirement, but the task succeeds only after several later actions. In BFCL-v4, an early tool call changes the filesystem used in later turns. In both cases, the effect of an action cannot be judged only from its immediate result. It also depends on whether the resulting interaction prefix makes eventual task completion more likely. This is the motivation for using Success Value in SCALE and for using its changes to construct Success-GAE.

The main difficulty is that a critic with aggregate return-prediction accuracy may still fail to resolve the local value differences needed to assign credit to actions , especially under sparse feedback and function approximation. Conventional critics estimate future return, but policy improvement also depends on knowing whether each intermediate decision makes task success more or less likely. We introduce SCALE , an actor–critic framework that augments conventional return estimation with explicit prediction of eventual task success. At each interaction prefix, the critic predicts a return value and a Success Value , defined as the probability that the task will eventually be completed from that prefix. SCALE converts changes in Success Value into multi-step action credit through Success-GAE and modulates its contribution according to the estimated reliability of the predictor, while retaining the token-level PPO objective. Across five agent benchmarks and three model backbones, SCALE improves task performance over the compared RL baselines in most settings, with gains of up to 4.1 percentage points in success rate. Separate critic-learning analyses show that SCALE also improves critic estimation and training stability. 1 1 footnotetext: Corresponding to Junchi Yan ( yanjunchi@sjtu.edu.cn ). 1 Introduction Figure 1: Comparison between PPO and SCALE . PPO derives step credit from changes in predicted return, which can be unreliable when feedback is sparse. An action may receive positive credit even when it lowers the probability of eventual success. SCALE instead uses changes in Success Value to measure whether each action makes task success more or less likely. Large language models (LLMs) are deployed as interactive agents that browse the web, use tools, and interact with environments over many steps ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Shridhar et al., 2021 ; Yao et al., 2022 ) . Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a framework for improving such agents from task outcomes ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Feng et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026b ) , yet it remains difficult to tell which intermediate actions help or hurt the outcome. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , an action can satisfy a local constraint yet make the task less likely to succeed. The learner therefore needs to determine which intermediate decisions improve the prospect of eventual task completion. For long-horizon language agents, this is difficult because supervision often arrives only after the entire interaction, while policy improvement depends on distinguishing the effects of individual decisions along the way. Existing methods assign credit at different parts of the trajectory. Standard PPO and outcome-based methods optimize token probabilities from trajectory-level returns ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) , while recent methods assign credit to individual turns or environment actions ( Zeng et al., 2025 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Ding et al., 2026 ) . Critic-based methods further estimate intermediate values to propagate delayed outcomes ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Kazemnejad et al., 2025 ; Hou et al., 2026 ) . These methods assign credit at finer parts of the trajectory, but accurate prediction of future return does not necessarily imply reliable action-level credit. Under sparse supervision and function approximation, a change in predicted return may not tell us whether a particular action made eventual success more likely. The central issue is therefore not only where credit is assigned, but whether the critic preserves the local ordering between alternative actions and whether its reliability can be assessed during training . In Sec. 3.2 , we show that this concern is practical rather than hypothetical, conventional PPO critics produce action-level credit that degrades toward random chance at long horizons and remains unstable throughout training, leaving reliable critic learning for long-horizon credit assignment an open challenge. To address these challenges, we introduce SCALE ( S uccess- C alibrated A dvantage L earning and E stimation), a success-aware actor–critic framework for long-horizon language agents. SCALE makes eventual task completion an explicit prediction target alongside conventional return estimation, rather than relying on return alone . Specifically, the critic retains a return head for expected cumulative reward and adds a Success Value head that estimates the probability of satisfying the benchmark’s terminal completion criterion from the current interaction prefix. It then uses changes in this prediction to assign credit to individual environment steps, reflecting whether each action improves eventual success. Because the reliability of this signal can vary during training, SCALE adjusts its contribution according to critic quality. The resulting credit complements the standard return-based advantage while retaining the token-level PPO objective. Sec. 4 details the framework. We evaluate SCALE on five representative agentic benchmarks spanning text-based interaction and tool use: ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ) , WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) , ScienceWorld ( Wang et al., 2022 ) , BFCL-v4 ( Patil et al., 2025 ) , and AppWorld ( Trivedi et al., 2024 ) . Across these tasks, SCALE consistently outperforms most strong agentic RL baselines and delivers substantial gains in task performance. Beyond end-task performance, We also analyze critic quality and the accuracy of its action credit to understand where these gains come from. Our contributions are threefold: ❶ Local-credit failure of return critics. We show that conventional PPO critics become less reliable at distinguishing alternative actions as decisions move farther from terminal supervision. ❷ Success-Based Credit with Reliability Control. We introduce SCALE , which explicitly predicts eventual task success from each interaction prefix and converts changes in this probability into multi-step action credit . It then modulates the contribution of this credit according to estimated critic reliability , while retaining the standard token-level PPO objective. ❸ Empirical validation. Experiments across five agent benchmarks and three model backbones show improvements in task performance, including gains of up to 4.1 percentage points in success rate. Additional analyses show improved action ranking and support the roles of success-based credit and reliability control. 2 Related Work Reinforcement Learning for LLM-based Agents. Reinforcement learning has evolved from preference alignment ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ) toward optimization from verifiable task outcomes ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , and has recently been extended to interactive language agents. Existing work studies RL for search and tool use ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Feng et al., 2026 ; Qian et al., 2025 ) , multi-turn environment interaction ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026b ) , and general agent-training frameworks ( Feng et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) . Scalable RL infrastructures such as verl ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) and ROLL ( Wang et al., 2025a ) support large-scale rollout generation and environment interaction. Other approaches improve long-horizon learning through planning and exploration ( Paglieri et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026d ; Wang et al., 2026c ) . While these methods improve the training and exploration of language agents, a central challenge remains: how to convert sparse trajectory-level outcomes into reliable credit for intermediate actions , particularly for decisions far from terminal supervision. Credit Assignment and Critic Learning. Existing approaches differ along two dimensions that are central to credit assignment: where credit is assigned along a trajectory and how that credit is estimated. Critic-free methods derive turn- or step-level signals through comparison, grouping, or structural information ( Zeng et al., 2025 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026d ) , but often require repeated states, milestones, or other task-dependent structure. Monte Carlo methods estimate local action values from multiple continuations, avoiding a learned critic at the cost of substantial sampling overhead ( Kazemnejad et al., 2025 ) . Critic-based methods instead propagate delayed outcomes through learned turn- or action-level values ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Tan et al., 2026 ) , but reliable local comparisons remain difficult when value estimates are learned from sparse supervision. Recent work further improves robustness by suppressing unreliable updates or controlling the use of uncertain credit signals ( Li et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2026b ; Tao et al., 2026 ) . In contrast, SCALE explicitly predicts eventual task success from each interaction prefix and uses the estimated reliability of this prediction to control its contribution to environment-step credit. Success-GAE uses changes in this prediction to compute step credit, and SCALE scales this credit according to the reliability of the success critic. We evaluate SCALE on five long-horizon agentic benchmarks spanning two major interaction paradigms. ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ) , WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) , and ScienceWorld ( Wang et al., 2022 ) represent text-based interactive environments, covering embodied household tasks, web navigation, and scientific reasoning. BFCL-v4 ( Patil et al., 2025 ) and AppWorld ( Trivedi et al., 2024 ) evaluate tool-using agents through function calling and application-level execution. These benchmarks let us test SCALE across different interaction structures, action spaces, and task horizons. Full benchmark details are provided in Appendix C . Baselines. We compare SCALE against representative prompting and RL baselines. Closed-source references include GPT-4o ( OpenAI, 2024 ) and Gemini-2.5-Pro ( Comanici et al., 2025 ) . Prompting baselines include Direct Prompt, ReAct ( Yao et al., 2023 ) , and Reflexion ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) . RL baselines cover three categories: (1) Standard policy optimization, including PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) , RLOO ( Ahmadian et al., 2024 ) , GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , and GSPO ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) ; (2) Fine-grained or structured credit assignment, including GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) , BEACON ( Wang et al., 2026d ) , ST-PPO ( Li et al., 2025a ) , and CAPO ( Wang et al., 2026a ) ; and (3) Critic-free sequence-level optimization, represented by SeeUPO ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . We use official implementations or closely follow the reported configurations whenever available. Implementation. Our experiments use Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , together with Qwen3-8B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , as backbone models. ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld are implemented with verl-agent ( Feng et al., 2025 ) , while BFCL-v4 and AppWorld are built on AgentEvolver ( Zhai et al., 2025 ) . We retain Qwen2.5 due to more stable agentic performance and infrastructure support, and use the same base model across RL methods for fair comparison. Within each backbone and benchmark setting, all trainable methods share the same initial model, rollout budget, environment interface, and evaluation protocol. Detailed configurations and hyperparameters are provided in Appendix C . 5.2 Main Results Text-Based Interactive Benchmarks. Table 2 reports results on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop. Overall, the results show that return estimation, success-based credit, and reliability weighting each play a distinct role in the full framework. 6 Conclusion We introduced SCALE for credit assignment in long-horizon language agents. Our analysis shows that a critic can retain aggregate return-prediction quality while becoming less reliable at ranking actions, especially for decisions far from terminal supervision. SCALE addresses this gap by predicting eventual task success, converting changes in this probability into multi-step action credit, and controlling its contribution according to predictor reliability. Across five agent benchmarks and three model backbones, SCALE improves task performance, while maintaining modest training overhead. These results show that improving local credit quality can benefit long-horizon policy learning without changing the underlying token-level PPO objective. Future work could explore incorporating richer signals into critic learning to improve reliability under long-horizon supervision. Appendix B Details of the Benchmarks We evaluate SCALE on five benchmarks spanning household interaction, web navigation, scientific experimentation, function calling, and application-level tool use. ALFWorld. ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ) is a text-based environment derived from ALFRED ( Shridhar et al., 2020 ) and TextWorld ( Côté et al., 2018 ) . An agent receives natural-language observations and must complete household tasks by navigating rooms and manipulating objects through textual commands. The benchmark includes tasks such as picking up, cleaning, heating, cooling, and examining objects. We use the standard benchmark split and report task success rate. WebShop. WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) simulates online shopping over a large collection of real products. Given a natural-language instruction, an agent searches for products, navigates product pages, selects options, and attempts to purchase an item that satisfies the requested attributes. The environment provides a graded task score based on how well the selected product matches the instruction, together with a binary success signal. We report both task score and success rate. ScienceWorld. ScienceWorld ( Wang et al., 2022 ) contains interactive science tasks in which an agent performs experiments and manipulates objects through natural-language actions. The tasks cover topics from physics, chemistry, and biology and require several dependent steps before the goal can be completed. We evaluate across the benchmark tasks and report both task score and success rate. BFCL-v4. BFCL-v4 ( Patil et al., 2025 ) evaluates the ability of language models to use external functions correctly. The agent must interpret a user request, choose appropriate functions, provide valid arguments, and use function outputs when further actions are required. This setting tests whether a policy can make reliable tool-use decisions over multiple interaction steps. We follow the benchmark evaluation protocol and report avg@4 together with pass@4 . AppWorld. AppWorld ( Trivedi et al., 2024 ) evaluates agents on tasks which interacts with APIs exposed by simulated applications. An agent must determine which applications and APIs are needed, execute sequences of calls, and use the returned information to complete the request. The tasks require dependent operations across applications, making successful completion sensitive to earlier decisions. We follow the standard evaluation protocol and report avg@4 together with pass@4 .
